chunks: "The biggest challenge is access. Modern boards have BGAs, inner layers and tiny pads, so you can't just touch the node you care about.
If the designer didn't add test points, you're stuck. Second is that the measurement changes the circuit.
A scope probe adds capacitance and resistance, a long ground lead rings and fakes noise, and a high-impedance node gets loaded by a multimeter.
So you can break something by measuring it, or see a problem that isn't there. Third is localising faults.
A short between two planes, an intermittent crack that only appears when warm, or a marginal timing bug that only shows at temperature are hard to find without a methodical approach.
Fourth is ambiguity: when it doesn't work, is it the hardware, the assembly, the firmware or my test setup?
I isolate by changing one thing at a time, comparing against a known-good board, and testing blocks separately.
And at scale there's cost and time: fixtures, programming, and getting good coverage without slowing the line."
